title: What are the core Kubernetes objects (Pod, Deployment, Service — ClusterIP/NodePort/LoadBalancer, Ingress, ConfigMap, Secret), and why are Pods treated as disposable "cattle, not pets"?
shortTitle: Core Kubernetes objects — Pod, Deployment, Service, Ingress, ConfigMap, Secret — and why Pods are "cattle, not pets"

s1_definition.profdef: The core Kubernetes objects are the building blocks you declare to run and expose an application. A Pod is the smallest deployable unit, wrapping one or more tightly-coupled containers that share a network address and storage. A Deployment manages a set of identical Pods through a ReplicaSet, handling scaling, rolling updates, and self-healing. A Service gives a stable virtual address and load-balances across the Pods behind it, in three types — ClusterIP for internal-only access, NodePort for exposing a port on every node, and LoadBalancer for a cloud external load balancer. An Ingress routes external HTTP traffic to Services by host and path. A ConfigMap holds non-secret configuration, and a Secret holds sensitive values like passwords, both injected into Pods as environment variables or mounted files. Pods are treated as disposable "cattle, not pets" because they are identical, replaceable, and expected to be killed and recreated at any time, so no state or identity lives in an individual Pod.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of National Bank of India's call centre. A Pod is one agent at a desk handling calls. A Deployment is the workforce manager who keeps exactly twenty agents on the floor, replacing anyone who goes home sick. A Service is the single phone number customers dial that quietly routes to whichever agent is free. An Ingress is the front switchboard that sends "loan queries" to the loans team and "card queries" to the cards team. A ConfigMap is the shared handbook of non-secret procedures, and a Secret is the sealed envelope with the vault combination. "Cattle, not pets" means the manager does not care which specific agent takes a call — any agent is interchangeable, and if one leaves, a replacement sits down immediately.
s1_definition.oneliner: Deployments keep interchangeable Pods running, Services give them a stable address, Ingress routes outside traffic in, ConfigMaps and Secrets feed them configuration, and no Pod is ever precious.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The core Kubernetes objects are the building blocks you declare to run and expose an application. A Pod is the smallest deployable unit, wrapping one or more tightly-coupled containers that share a network address and storage. A Deployment manages a set of identical Pods through a ReplicaSet, handling scaling, rolling updates, and self-healing. A Service gives a stable virtual address and load-balances across the Pods behind it, in three types — ClusterIP for internal-only access, NodePort for exposing a port on every node, and LoadBalancer for a cloud external load balancer. An Ingress routes external HTTP traffic to Services by host and path. A ConfigMap holds non-secret configuration, and a Secret holds sensitive values like passwords, both injected into Pods as environment variables or mounted files. Pods are treated as disposable "cattle, not pets" because they are identical, replaceable, and expected to be killed and recreated at any time, so no state or identity lives in an individual Pod.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of National Bank of India's call centre. A Pod is one agent at a desk handling calls. A Deployment is the workforce manager who keeps exactly twenty agents on the floor, replacing anyone who goes home sick. A Service is the single phone number customers dial that quietly routes to whichever agent is free. An Ingress is the front switchboard that sends "loan queries" to the loans team and "card queries" to the cards team. A ConfigMap is the shared handbook of non-secret procedures, and a Secret is the sealed envelope with the vault combination. "Cattle, not pets" means the manager does not care which specific agent takes a call — any agent is interchangeable, and if one leaves, a replacement sits down immediately.

**One line to remember:** Deployments keep interchangeable Pods running, Services give them a stable address, Ingress routes outside traffic in, ConfigMaps and Secrets feed them configuration, and no Pod is ever precious.

sections.s2_technical:
A Pod is the atom of scheduling in Kubernetes. It wraps one or more containers that must run together on the same node, sharing an IP address, network namespace, and often a volume. Most Pods run a single application container, sometimes with a helper sidecar such as a logging agent. A Pod is ephemeral: it has no durable identity, and when it dies Kubernetes does not resurrect that exact Pod; it creates a brand-new one with a new IP. This is why you almost never create Pods directly in production.

A Deployment is the object you actually declare. It wraps a ReplicaSet, which ensures a specified number of identical Pods are always running. The Deployment adds update strategy on top: when you change the Pod template, such as pointing to a new image version, it performs a controlled rollout and can roll back. It also provides self-healing: if a Pod crashes or a node dies, the ReplicaSet notices the actual count is below the desired count and creates replacements. You declare the desired state, and the controller continuously reconciles reality toward it.

A Service solves the problem that Pod IPs are unstable. Because Pods come and go with new IPs, you cannot hardcode a Pod's address. A Service provides a stable virtual IP and DNS name and load-balances requests across all healthy Pods that match its label selector. There are three main types. ClusterIP, the default, gives an address reachable only inside the cluster, which is how microservices call each other. NodePort opens the same port on every node's IP, making the Service reachable from outside the cluster for simple cases. LoadBalancer provisions a cloud provider's external load balancer with a public address, the normal way to expose a Service to the internet on a managed cluster.

An Ingress operates at the HTTP layer above Services. Instead of exposing many LoadBalancers, you run one Ingress controller and declare rules that route by hostname and URL path: requests to the transfers host and path go to the transfer Service, requests to the accounts path go to the accounts Service. Ingress typically also terminates TLS, so one entry point handles certificates for many backend Services.

A ConfigMap stores non-sensitive configuration as key-value pairs, such as a feature flag, a log level, or a downstream URL. A Secret stores sensitive data such as database passwords and API keys; it is base64-encoded and, in a hardened cluster, encrypted at rest and tightly access-controlled. Both are injected into Pods either as environment variables or as files mounted into the container, which keeps configuration out of the image so the same image runs unchanged across environments with different config.

The "cattle, not pets" philosophy is the mental model that makes all of this work. A pet is a server you name, care for individually, and nurse back to health when sick. Cattle are a herd of identical, numbered animals; if one is unwell you replace it rather than treating it. Kubernetes Pods are cattle: they are identical, disposable, and replaceable, so Kubernetes can freely kill and recreate them during scaling, updates, node maintenance, or failure. The practical consequences are strict: applications must be stateless or externalise their state to a database or object store, must start quickly, and must shut down gracefully, because any Pod can vanish at any moment. Persistent identity, when genuinely needed, is handled by a different object called a StatefulSet, precisely because ordinary Pods have none.

The senior-level nuance is that this entire model is declarative and reconciliation-driven. You never tell Kubernetes the steps to take; you declare the desired end state in YAML, and controllers continuously work to make the actual state match. That is why self-healing, scaling, and rolling updates all emerge from the same core idea, and why treating Pods as disposable is not a limitation but the foundation of the system's resilience.
sections.s3_banking:
At National Bank of India, the Transfer Service runs on Kubernetes. The team needs it to survive node failures, scale under load, be reachable at a stable address, route external customer traffic correctly, and read its configuration and database password without baking them into the image.

Problem 1 — A node hosting a Transfer Service Pod suddenly fails at midnight. If the team had created that Pod by hand, the service would simply be down until someone noticed. This is exactly the problem a Deployment solves: it keeps the desired number of Pods running and recreates any that vanish, so the service self-heals without a human.

Problem 2 — Other services, like the Fraud Service, need to call the Transfer Service, but Pod IPs change every time a Pod is recreated. This is exactly the problem a ClusterIP Service solves: it gives a stable name and load-balances across whatever Pods currently exist.

Problem 3 — The Transfer Service needs a log level and a downstream URL that differ per environment, plus a database password that must never appear in the image or in git. This is exactly what ConfigMap and Secret solve: configuration and secrets are injected at runtime, so the same image is promoted everywhere unchanged.

To make this runnable without a real cluster, we will build a small program that models these objects in memory. It will contain a `Pod` with an IP and a liveness flag, a `Deployment` that keeps a desired replica count alive and recreates dead Pods, a `Service` that load-balances across live Pods by returning their IPs round-robin, and a `ConfigStore` modelling a merged ConfigMap and Secret. The demo creates a Deployment of three Pods, routes some requests through the Service, kills a Pod to show self-healing, and reads config and a secret, printing each step so the roles of the objects are visible.
sections.s4a_structure:
Project structure:

```
k8s-model/
├── pom.xml
├── manifests/
│   ├── deployment.yml
│   ├── service.yml
│   ├── ingress.yml
│   ├── configmap.yml
│   └── secret.yml
├── src/
│   ├── main/
│   │   ├── java/com/bank/k8s/
│   │   │   ├── K8sDemo.java                       (main class)
│   │   │   ├── model/
│   │   │   │   └── Pod.java
│   │   │   ├── controller/
│   │   │   │   └── Deployment.java                (reconciles desired count)
│   │   │   ├── network/
│   │   │   │   └── Service.java                   (load-balances live Pods)
│   │   │   └── config/
│   │   │       └── ConfigStore.java               (ConfigMap + Secret)
│   │   └── resources/
│   │       └── application.yml
│   └── test/
│       └── java/com/bank/k8s/
│           └── controller/
│               └── DeploymentTest.java
```

The manifests are part of the deliverable:

```yaml
# manifests/deployment.yml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: transfer-service
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels: { app: transfer-service }
  template:
    metadata:
      labels: { app: transfer-service }
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: transfer-service
          image: registry.bank.local/transfer-service:2.4.0
          envFrom:
            - configMapRef: { name: transfer-config }   # non-secret config
            - secretRef:    { name: transfer-secret }    # DB password etc.
---
# manifests/service.yml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: transfer-service
spec:
  type: ClusterIP                 # internal-only; Fraud Service calls this
  selector: { app: transfer-service }
  ports: [{ port: 80, targetPort: 8080 }]
---
# manifests/ingress.yml
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: bank-ingress
spec:
  rules:
    - host: api.bank.local
      http:
        paths:
          - path: /transfers
            pathType: Prefix
            backend: { service: { name: transfer-service, port: { number: 80 } } }
---
# manifests/configmap.yml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata: { name: transfer-config }
data:
  LOG_LEVEL: "INFO"
  FRAUD_SERVICE_URL: "http://fraud-service"
---
# manifests/secret.yml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata: { name: transfer-secret }
type: Opaque
data:
  DB_PASSWORD: czNjcjN0UGFzcw==    # base64-encoded value
```
sections.s4e_build:
How you build and run it:

```bash
# Build and run the model
mvn clean package -DskipTests
java -jar target/k8s-model-1.0.0.jar

# Apply the real objects to a cluster
kubectl apply -f manifests/
kubectl get pods,svc,ingress
# Prove self-healing: delete a pod and watch a replacement appear
kubectl delete pod -l app=transfer-service --field-selector ... 
kubectl get pods -w
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a Deployment with a desired count of three Pods, a Service in front of them, a few routed requests, a simulated node failure, and a ConfigMap plus Secret read at the end.

Step 1: The Deployment is created with a desired count of three. Its reconcile loop sees zero live Pods against a desired three, so it creates three Pods, each with a generated name and an IP such as 10.0.0.10 through 10.0.0.12.

Step 2: The Service receives three requests. It round-robins across the three live Pods, returning a different Pod IP each time. The caller never needs to know the individual IPs; it only talks to the Service.

Step 3: A node fails, modelled by killing the first Pod. That Pod is now marked not alive. At this instant the live count has dropped to two, below the desired three.

Step 4: The Deployment's reconcile loop runs again. It removes the dead Pod from its list and, seeing only two live Pods against a desired three, creates a brand-new Pod with a new name and a new IP. This is self-healing with no human involved. Note the replacement is a different Pod with a different IP, which is precisely the cattle-not-pets principle in action.

Step 5: The Service routes another request. Because it selects from the currently live Pods, it may now route to the freshly created Pod. The stable Service address absorbed the Pod churn completely, so callers saw no disruption.

Step 6: The ConfigStore is read. Asking for the LOG_LEVEL returns INFO from the ConfigMap and logs the value, because it is not sensitive. Asking for DB_PASSWORD resolves the value from the Secret but logs only a masked placeholder, because secret values must never appear in logs.

Final output:

```text

INFO: created pod transfer-c3d4e @ 10.0.0.11
INFO: created pod transfer-e5f6a @ 10.0.0.12
INFO: service routed request -> transfer-a1b2c @ 10.0.0.10
INFO: service routed request -> transfer-c3d4e @ 10.0.0.11
INFO: service routed request -> transfer-e5f6a @ 10.0.0.12
```

```text
  Customer: GET https://api.bank.local/transfers
    │
    ▼
  Ingress (api.bank.local, path /transfers, TLS terminated)
    │ routes by host+path
    ▼
  Service: transfer-service (ClusterIP, stable virtual IP)
    │ load-balances across label app=transfer-service
    ├──────────────┬──────────────┐
    ▼              ▼              ▼
  Pod @10.0.0.10  Pod @.11       Pod @.12     ← managed by Deployment (replicas=3)
    │              │              │
    │  each Pod reads config at startup:
    │   envFrom ConfigMap(transfer-config): LOG_LEVEL, FRAUD_SERVICE_URL
    │   envFrom Secret(transfer-secret):    DB_PASSWORD
    ▼
  ─── node failure ───
  Pod @10.0.0.10 dies  →  Deployment reconcile  →  new Pod @10.0.0.12 created

```

```text
  │ + reconcile()        │       └──────────────────────┘
  │ + livePods()         │
  │ + killOne()          │
  └──────────┬───────────┘
             │ queried by
             ▼
  ┌──────────────────────┐       ┌──────────────────────┐
  │   Service            │       │   ConfigStore        │
  │ - counter: AtomicInt │       │ - configMap: Map     │
  │ + route(): String    │       │ - secret: Map        │

                                  └──────────────────────┘

  [Pending] → [Running] → [Terminating] → [gone]

  ── Call Chain ──────────────────────────────────────────
  1. new Deployment(3) → reconcile() → 3 Pods created
  2. Service.route() ×3 → round-robin across live Pods
  3. Deployment.killOne() → reconcile() → replacement Pod created
  4. Service.route() → routes to a live Pod transparently
  5. ConfigStore.config("LOG_LEVEL") / secret("DB_PASSWORD")
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The core Kubernetes objects each solve a specific problem. A Pod is the smallest deployable unit, wrapping one or more containers that share a network address and storage; it is ephemeral and gets a fresh IP whenever it is created. A Deployment is what I actually declare: it manages a set of identical Pods through a ReplicaSet, keeps the desired number running, performs controlled rolling updates, and self-heals by recreating any Pod that dies. A Service solves the problem that Pod IPs are unstable — it gives a stable virtual address and DNS name and load-balances across all healthy Pods matching its label selector. It comes in three types: ClusterIP for internal-only communication between microservices, NodePort to expose a port on every node, and LoadBalancer to provision a cloud external load balancer with a public address.

Above Services, an Ingress routes external HTTP traffic by hostname and path to the right Service and usually terminates TLS, so one entry point serves many backends. A ConfigMap holds non-secret configuration like log levels and downstream URLs, and a Secret holds sensitive values like database passwords, and both are injected into Pods as environment variables or mounted files. That keeps configuration out of the container image, which is why I can build one image and promote it unchanged from development to production, with only the config and secrets differing per environment.

The reason Pods are treated as cattle, not pets, is that they are identical, disposable, and replaceable. A pet is a server you name and nurse back to health; cattle are a numbered herd where a sick animal is replaced, not treated. Kubernetes freely kills and recreates Pods during scaling, updates, node maintenance, and failures, so the application must externalise its state to a database or object store, start quickly, and shut down gracefully, because any Pod can vanish at any time. When genuine per-instance identity is required, that is handled by a StatefulSet, precisely because ordinary Pods have none.

At National Bank of India, this model is what let the Transfer Service survive a midnight node failure with no human intervention. The Pod on the failed node vanished, the Deployment's reconciliation loop noticed the live count had fallen below the desired three, and it created a replacement Pod with a new IP within seconds. The Service in front absorbed the churn completely because it always routes to whatever Pods are currently live, so other services calling the stable Service name never noticed. The whole system is declarative — I describe the desired end state in YAML and controllers continuously reconcile reality toward it — and treating Pods as disposable is not a limitation but the very foundation of that resilience.
